# Evaluating Retrieval Across Domains — abstract-only assessment

Synthetic PoC research; not a real-world source assessment.
Source: https://research.example.test/new-evaluation

## Assessment
Experimental evidence first: the accessible abstract states, “The abstract claims retrieval improves results across five domains.” This is a reported cross-domain result, but the accessible material does not provide enough experimental detail to independently assess its strength: “It supplies no sample size, confidence intervals, baseline details, or method section.” Accordingly, the abstract is directionally consistent with the paper’s conclusion that retrieval improves results, but it does not demonstrate the magnitude, uncertainty, comparator, design, or causal basis needed to substantiate that conclusion. Access is explicitly abstract-only: “Only the abstract is available in this fixture; the full paper is inaccessible.” No related topic notes were supplied, so no external contextual connections are asserted.

### The accessible abstract reports that retrieval improves results across five domains.
> The abstract claims retrieval improves results across five domains.

This is the central reported finding and is evidence only at the level of an abstract assertion. It supports the paper’s conclusion directionally, but the available text does not report effect sizes or domain-specific results.

### The accessible source omits sample size, confidence intervals, baseline details, and a method section.
> It supplies
no sample size, confidence intervals, baseline details, or method section.

These omissions prevent evaluation of statistical precision, comparison conditions, study design, replication details, and whether the reported improvement warrants causal attribution. No missing values or procedures are inferred.

### Only the abstract is accessible; the full paper is unavailable.
> Only the abstract is available in this fixture; the full paper is inaccessible.

This assessment is limited to abstract coverage and does not represent a full-text review.

## Limitations
- Only abstract-level access was available; the source states, “Only the abstract is available in this fixture; the full paper is inaccessible.”
- Critical evaluation details are absent; the source states, “It supplies
no sample size, confidence intervals, baseline details, or method section.”
- The phrase “retrieval improves results” reports an improvement, but without methods or comparator details the assessment cannot determine whether this is a causal effect rather than an observed association or benchmark difference.
- No sample sizes, confidence intervals, baselines, methods, effect magnitudes, domain identities, or domain-level results are inferred.

## Connections

Disposition: Archive as an abstract-only, limited-support assessment. # Synthetic research fixture assessment: Memory Retrieval and Agent Success

Synthetic PoC research; not a real-world source assessment.
Source: https://papers.example.test/controlled-memory
Source SHA-256: 2b3d517422e10acc09940a757d9ff47c3a3b49136b1362ff0d6317bce4db3043
Read at: 2026-09-16T10:39:09.388Z
Coverage: full_text

## Assessment
This synthetic research fixture reports that agent success rose from 58% to 71% on 120 synthetic tasks when a no-retrieval/free-text baseline was replaced by a treatment that jointly added retrieval and a structured answer format. The comparison supports an observed association between the bundled treatment and higher success on this task set, but it does not identify retrieval as the cause because answer formatting changed simultaneously and no format ablation was run. Experimental validity is further limited by three repetitions on the same 120-task set, no confidence interval, no held-out set, unavailable code and raw per-task outcomes, and no measurement of production generalization or cost. Accordingly, the authors’ retrieval-specific causal attribution is stronger than the reported design supports.

### The document is explicitly a synthetic research fixture rather than a real published paper.
> SYNTHETIC RESEARCH FIXTURE, not a published paper.

This label governs how the source should be represented; it should not be treated as real-world published research.

### The principal reported finding is an increase in success from 58% to 71%.
> Results: Success increased from 58% to 71%.

This is the reported outcome difference. It is an observation from the comparison, not by itself evidence that retrieval alone caused the increase.

### The evaluation used 120 synthetic tasks and the same base model.
> Methods: We evaluated 120 synthetic tasks with the same base model.

Holding the base model constant removes one possible source of variation, but it does not resolve the simultaneous retrieval-and-format intervention.

### The baseline and treatment differ on both retrieval and output format.
> The baseline
used no retrieval and a free-text answer format. The treatment added retrieval
and a structured answer format.

Because retrieval and structured formatting changed together, the experiment tests a bundled intervention. It cannot isolate a retrieval-specific effect.

### The study did not perform an ablation of the format change.
> We did not ablate the format change.

Without retrieval-only, format-only, or factorial comparison arms, there is no direct estimate separating retrieval from formatting.

### The same task set was reused for three repetitions.
> Three repetitions used the same
task set.

Repeated runs can show run-to-run behavior on those tasks, but reuse does not supply independent task-set replication or evidence of generalization to new tasks.

### No confidence interval and no held-out task set were reported.
> No confidence interval or held-out task set was reported.

The source therefore gives no reported interval estimate for uncertainty and no held-out evaluation for assessing performance on an unseen task set.

### The authors attribute the improvement to retrieval.
> Conclusion: The authors attribute the improvement to retrieval.

This is the source’s causal conclusion, but the design described in the source does not isolate retrieval from the concurrent format change.

### The source itself identifies the format change as a confound and rejects a retrieval-alone causal inference.
> Limitations: The simultaneous format change is a confound. The result cannot
establish that retrieval alone caused the gain.

This directly limits the strength of support for the conclusion: the evidence supports a gain for the combined treatment, not a causal effect of retrieval alone.

### Production generalization and cost were not measured.
> Production generalization and
cost were not measured.

The fixture supplies no evidence that the result transfers to production settings and no basis for evaluating computational or operational tradeoffs.

### Code and raw per-task outcomes are unavailable.
> Code and raw per-task outcomes are unavailable.

Independent reproduction and task-level error, variance, and sensitivity analyses cannot be performed from the supplied materials.

### The abstract cautiously states that retrieval appears to improve task completion.
> Abstract: A retrieval system appears to improve agent task completion.

The word “appears” preserves some uncertainty, but the experiment only supports an association with the combined retrieval-plus-structured-format treatment.

## Limitations
- Structured-format confound: retrieval and answer format changed simultaneously, so the observed 58%-to-71% difference belongs to a bundled intervention.
- No ablation: the source states that it did not ablate the format change, leaving retrieval-only and formatting-only effects unidentified.
- Repeated use of the same 120-task set: three repetitions do not constitute evaluation on independently sampled or unseen tasks.
- No confidence interval: the reported percentages are not accompanied by interval uncertainty.
- No held-out set: generalization to unseen synthetic tasks was not tested.
- Unavailable code and raw per-task outcomes: reproduction and granular outcome analysis are not possible from the source.
- No production-generalization measurement: the synthetic-task result does not establish production performance.
- No cost measurement: the evaluation does not quantify the resource or operational cost of adding retrieval.

## Connections
- Retrieval-augmented agents: this design evaluates retrieval only as part of a bundle with structured output, so it is informative about the bundle but not the retrieval component in isolation.
- Controlled experiments and causal inference: keeping the base model fixed is a control, but causal identification still fails when two treatment dimensions—retrieval and format—change at once.
- Ablation studies: a retrieval-only arm, a structured-format-only arm, and a combined arm would separate component effects; the source explicitly says, “We did not ablate the format change.”
- Evaluation validity: reuse of one 120-task set, absence of a held-out set and confidence interval, and unavailable task-level outcomes constrain uncertainty assessment, reproducibility, and evidence for generalization.
- External and operational validity: because “Production generalization and cost were not measured,” the fixture does not support claims about deployment performance or cost-effectiveness.

Disposition: Archive as a synthetic, source-grounded critical assessment. Treat the 58%-to-71% increase as a reported association for the combined retrieval-plus-structured-format intervention on the repeated 120-task set. Do not attribute the gain to retrieval alone; the missing format ablation and other evaluation limitations make the retrieval-specific conclusion unsupported by the reported experiment.
